meta_title: Install VpnHood! SERVER with Docker | VpnHood!
meta_description: Install VpnHood! SERVER as a Docker container on Linux with one command, standalone or from VpnHood! MANAGER. The container keeps the server up to date.
title: Install VpnHood! SERVER with Docker
lead: Run the server as a container on any Linux machine with Docker. One command installs it, as a managed server or a standalone one, and the container keeps the server running and up to date.
req_machine: A Linux machine with a public IP address, on x64 or arm64. The image is built for both.
req_docker: Docker with its compose plugin. The installer can install it for you on Ubuntu, Debian and the distributions based on them.
req_port: TCP port [server_port] open, both in the machine's firewall and in your hosting provider's. The container shares the host's network, so the server listens on the host's port directly.
mgr_box_title: Easily add, manage and monitor your servers with VpnHood! MANAGER
mgr_box_desc: Instead of running the commands below, let the free web panel install the server's container for you. It issues the access keys, and shows each server's status and what each key uses.
step_install_run: Run this command. It asks whether to install Docker, then downloads the compose file and starts the server's container.
step_install_options: To install it in a script, without the question, see Installer options.
step_install_storage: The server keeps its settings, keys and logs in [server_storage] on the host, so they outlive the container.
step_key_run: Run this on the machine. The key is made inside the server's container, so it uses the server's own settings.
step_key_same: The output and the options are the same as for a standalone server installed without Docker: copy the line under [accesskey_heading], and see Create your first access key for the options that limit a key.
caption_example: For example, a key for one phone
step_connect: Install VpnHood! CLIENT on each device, add the key, and connect.
manage_title: Start, stop and check the server
manage_desc: The container is called [docker_container]. Docker starts it again when the machine restarts, and inside it the server is started again if it crashes.
manage_log: The same log is written to [server_log] on the host.
settings_file: The server reads its settings from [server_appsettings]. Edit the file, then restart the container with [docker_restart].
settings_env: Where you cannot edit a file, put the whole content of an appsettings.json in the [env_appsettings] environment variable instead. The server then uses it in place of the file.
settings_more: Set your server's IP addresses and Use a domain name and a trusted certificate walk through the settings you are most likely to change.
updates_auto: The server updates itself inside the container. It checks for a new release when it starts and every 12 hours, and restarts into the new version.
updates_off: To stay on one version, set [env_auto_update_off] in the container's environment.
updates_image: Now and then a release needs a newer image. The server then keeps its current version, and its log says [log_pull_image] Run the install command again: it pulls the latest image and creates the container again, with the same settings and keys.
updates_old: If you installed with an earlier version of the script, run the install command again. It moves the server to the new image and removes the old [old_updater_container] container.
uninstall_run: To remove the server, remove its container and its image. Its settings, access keys and certificates stay in [server_storage] on the host, for a later install.
uninstall_caption_purge: Delete its settings and keys too: devices that hold its keys can no longer connect, even to a new install
manual_desc: If you manage your containers by hand, this is the container the installer creates. Run it on the host's network, as the installer does.
manual_update: To move it to a newer image, pull [docker_image] and create the container again.
